summary.summary: Cover report for Sandwell's draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, published on the council website on 30 June 2026 in line with the statutory deadline; Grant Thornton began fieldwork on 13 July 2026, targeting audit completion by 10 November and final publication by 30 November 2026, well inside the 31 January 2027 backstop. The draft CIES reports net income of £109.6m, with General Fund balances up £10.6m, HRA balances down £1.1m and capital-programme reserves up £15.8m — a strengthening usable-reserves position. One open item: a specialist adviser is reviewing all four PFI financial models for consistency and compliance, and the council cannot yet quantify what adjustments that review will feed into the final accounts. Group accounts consolidate the wholly-owned Sandwell Children's Trust.

signals.headline: Draft 2025/26 accounts published 30 June 2026 on the statutory deadline; General Fund balances improved £10.6m, but a review of four PFI financial models is ongoing with the impact not yet quantifiable
signals.why: The reserves direction is positive for creditors, but the PFI model review is an open-ended adjustment risk sitting in the draft until the November 2026 audit completion.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio returned 4.10%, marginally above the 4.01% benchmark, on average balances of £79.7m
findings.detail: The council's investment strategy prioritised security and liquidity over yield. The portfolio was maintained short-term to cover cash flow requirements, with consideration given to placements up to 12 months with high credit-rated institutions. The 4.10% return slightly outperformed the benchmark of 4.01%, indicating competent treasury management of investment balances.
findings.matters: Returns on investment balances offset some of the cost of internal borrowing (borrowing from cash reserves rather than external markets). The benchmark outperformance is modest but shows the council is not losing return through conservative positioning.
findings.figures: Portfolio return 4.10%; benchmark 4.01%. Average balances invested £79.7m. Year-end investment balance £44.9m.
findings.quote: Returns on the investment portfolio have been marginally above benchmark with 2025-26 posting an average return of 4.10% (with average balances invested of £79.7m) against a benchmark of 4.01%.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £35.7m in prudential borrowing caused the CFR variance, with works reprofiled into future years
findings.detail: The council forecast prudential borrowing of £69.066m in its February 2026 Treasury Management Strategy but only £33.383m was required. The difference is attributed to phasing delays and schemes not commencing as planned, with works being reprofiled into future financial years. Despite the slippage, the overall capital programme remained within approved budgets.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage can indicate either disciplined project management or delays in delivering services to residents. A lender needs to understand whether delays are temporary repricing or signal broader issues with project delivery. The reprofiling defers the borrowing need but does not eliminate it.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing actual £33.383m vs forecast £69.066m. Variance £35.683m (51.6% lower than forecast).
findings.quote: Key variances from the approved indicators in 2025-26 are due to the slippage of capital expenditure into future financial years due to phasing of works on schemes being reprofiled or schemes not commencing.

findings.headline: Council took no material new external borrowing in 2025-26 due to inflated borrowing rates; instead took short-dated debt (2 months to 2 years) at rates 4.04–5.00% with view to future refinancing
findings.detail: Rather than lock in long-term debt at high rates, the council took short-dated borrowing from PWLB and other local authorities maturing between June 2026 and March 2028. This included £60m from PWLB (HRA and General Fund) and £50m from other local authorities (General Fund), all at rates between 4.04% and 5.00%. The strategy assumes rates will fall, allowing refinancing at better terms when debt matures.
findings.matters: This exposes the council to refinancing risk when the short-dated debt matures. If rates remain elevated or rise further, refinancing costs will be higher, pushing up future financing costs. It also shows the council is deferring the cost decision rather than locking in rates now.
findings.figures: New borrowing in 2025-26: PWLB HRA £40m at 4.04-4.10%; PWLB GF £20m at 4.30-4.33%; Other Local Auth GF £50m at 4.10-5.00%. Rates ranging 4.04% to 5.00%. Maturities 2 months to 2 years.
findings.quote: It was considered prudent to take short-dated debt with the view that at maturity it could be refinanced at a more preferential rate.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 Leases implementation added £14.567m to long-term liabilities, larger than the £6.995m initially forecast
findings.detail: The new accounting standard (effective 1 April 2024) required the council to recognise lease assets and future payment liabilities on the balance sheet. The actual movement was significantly larger than the initial forecast because the council lacked data to quantify the impact when the forecast was made. Liabilities are paid through annual unitary charges, lease payments, and service costs but have no impact on budgets.
findings.matters: This increases the reported liabilities on the council's balance sheet but does not represent new cash obligations—it is a reclassification of existing lease commitments. However, it materially affects balance sheet ratios and the CFR that lenders and auditors monitor, and the underestimation shows data weaknesses in the council's accounting systems.
findings.figures: Actual movement in other long-term liabilities (£14.567m); forecast movement (£6.995m). Difference of £7.572m larger than expected.
findings.quote: The movement in other long-term liabilities is larger than original estimates as these originally did not include values for the implementation of IFRS 16 – Leases due to us not having the data to quantify the financial impact.

findings.headline: Council maintained under-borrowed position by borrowing internally from cash reserves rather than accessing external debt markets
findings.detail: The council's gross borrowing (£526.057m) remains below the Capital Financing Requirement (£904.045m), a strategic under-borrowed position of £377.988m. The council chose not to take new external borrowing despite capital financing needs, instead drawing on internal cash resources. This generates cash efficiencies in a high interest rate environment but requires careful cash management and monitoring of liquidity.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing can be prudent cash management in high rate environments but also represents deferred external borrowing costs. A lender needs to assess whether the council can sustain this position and whether refinancing risk is building as short-dated debt approaches maturity.
findings.figures: Over/(Under) Borrowing position: (£377.988m). Gross borrowing £526.057m vs CFR £904.045m. External borrowings £441.688m; other liabilities £84.369m.
findings.quote: For all financial years detailed above, the Council has held an under-borrowed position when comparing actual debt holdings to the Capital Financing Requirement. This is a strategic application of treasury cash management as the Council has borrowed "internally" from its cash investment resources, thereby reducing investment income opportunity but also not incurring increased debt costs.
